SK2102 The [DebuggerDisplay] string names a member that does not exist

A {…} hole in a [DebuggerDisplay] string on a type declaration names a single identifier that is not a member of that type or of anything it inherits or implements.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since1.3
SupersedesS4545

Why

The expression is bound by the debugger at inspection time, not by the compiler, so a rename breaks it silently and it is discovered while debugging something else, at the moment it is least welcome. It is the same string-to-member binding nameof exists to remove, and the same class of defect as an ArgumentException naming a parameter that is not there. There is no fix: only the author knows which member was meant, and a rule that guessed would rename the display to whatever happened to be nearby.

Example

Instead of:

[DebuggerDisplay("{Title,nq}")]
sealed class Book {
    public string Name { get; init; } = "";
}

Write:

[DebuggerDisplay("{Name,nq}")]
sealed class Book {
    public string Name { get; init; } = "";
}

When it does not fire

⚠ The text inside the braces is a limited expression language, not a member name, and a parser that guesses at it produces false positives on correct code. The accepted grammar is therefore deliberately tiny: one identifier, with an optional this. in front and an optional ,nq-style all-letters format specifier behind. ⚠ Anything else withdraws the whole attribute rather than the one hole — a call, an index, an operator, a literal, a further ., a nested brace, an unbalanced brace, a comma this parser cannot account for. A string this parser only half understands is a string it has no standing to report on. ⚠ The dotted path is the exclusion that matters most: {Owner.Name} would need the member's type to answer and {DateTime.Now} has a root that is not a member of anything, so reporting either would be wrong for a different reason each time. ⚠ The lookup searches implemented interfaces as well as base types, and a sabotage that failed to fail is what established that this is the guard doing the work. The first version also matched a mangled explicit-implementation name — ICollection.Count ends with .Count — on the reasoning that a plain lookup misses an explicit implementation. The reasoning is true and the code was still redundant: an explicit implementation requires the interface to be in AllInterfaces, where the member is declared under its plain name, so the two guards covered exactly the same cases and neither could be broken into failing, each masking the other. The mangled match was removed as having no case of its own; the interface walk has one — a default interface member, which the type does not declare at all — and there is now a fixture that only it can save. An error type anywhere on the base or interface chain withdraws the answer entirely — an unresolved base reads as "no such member" and reporting it would be silently wrong, which is also why the rule finds nothing on a source slice with no dependency closure (#277). Only a class, struct, record or record struct declaration is examined; [DebuggerDisplay] also targets a field, a property and an assembly, and on those the expression binds against something other than the annotated declaration. The argument must be a compile-time constant string. Generated code is excluded.
